paragraphs: I am 上岡優介, and from March 2023 I did a clerkship for one month in infectious diseases at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore in the United States. Although it was a short period of one month, I had a valuable and irreplaceable experience. I would like to introduce my clerkship life and daily life.

Because this study abroad was resuming for the first time in four years after COVID, the preparation before going was extremely difficult. Within Nagoya University it had been decided that I could study at Johns Hopkins, but notice of acceptance never actually came from the other side's academic office, and even one month before the planned study abroad it was undecided whether I could really go. I called the person in charge directly and acceptance was somehow decided, but after that I frantically began preparations for living.

Perhaps because the acceptance period had been shortened from the previous two to three months to one month, the fee for the hospital-affiliated dormitory had become so high that I could not possibly pay it, so I gave up on living in the dormitory. I searched for a monthly apartment near the university and corresponded with the landlord, and somehow secured a place to live, and decided to share a house with a classmate who was going on the study abroad with me, but because I had heard that Baltimore, where the university is, is a place with poor public safety, my worry about whether I could live there and come back safely only kept piling up.

This time I was allowed to do my clerkship in infectious diseases at Bayview Medical Center, a branch hospital of Johns Hopkins University. This hospital is 20 minutes by bus from the main hospital, and compared with the main hospital with its many complex operations and diseases, it was like a fortress accepting local residents with a wide range from mild to severe.

In infectious diseases, we do consult work for complicated infectious disease care, such as infections with many complications and severe sepsis and bacteremia. A young fellow (what in Japan would be a senior resident) and a veteran attending (what in Japan would be a supervising doctor) work as a team, handling an average of about four consults every day. Among the consulted patients, those whose condition has settled or for whom it takes time to establish a treatment plan are taken on by infectious diseases as a secondary service.

The flow of the day was as follows. First thing in the morning, we check the consults that came in from the previous evening to the morning, and grasp from the chart the patient's background, the course up to admission, current test results and the reason for the consult. The fellow goes around examining patients in the morning, and after a conference with the attending and the infectious disease pharmacist first thing in the afternoon, the whole team rounds on the patients again in the afternoon. The consulted patients' locations were scattered from general wards to the ICU and CCU and sometimes the emergency department, and the backs of the doctors, walking around the whole hospital and giving accurate advice while communicating with the doctors and nurses of each department, looked very dazzling.

As for the clerkship content, it began with following behind the doctor and observing examinations and conferences. On the first day, I was handed the list of the doctor's assigned patients and told "I'm going to examine them now, follow me," and I followed, but the first hospital was like a maze, the doctor's explanations were too fast and I could not catch even half, and I did not know what to ask even when I wanted to ask a question; it was a terrible start. I remember feeling a strong sense of crisis that the clerkship would end with my gaining nothing.

So, in order to increase what I could do little by little, I came to the hospital earlier than the doctors and gathered patient information from the chart, looked up standard treatment in Up-To-Date while eating lunch, looked for something, anything, to ask the doctors, and continued days of asking questions during conferences and rounds. In the United States, among hospitals using the same electronic medical record system, one can see the same patient's admission records and culture tests at other hospitals. It is convenient, but the information is cluttered, and it took time to find even a single item of past history or antibiotic use history needed for examination.

From the second week I actually took charge of patients, and at first I watched the fellow examining and at the conference I presented the fellow's examination content and the chart information. Gradually I began taking histories from patients in front of the fellow, but I could not move the conversation along well and was often interrupted by the senior doctor in the middle of history taking, and frustrating days continued. As I took notes on how the doctor talked to patients, what he asked, and the points he focused on at conferences, and imitated them right away, I gradually came to be entrusted with "go take the history from the patient by yourself." In the end I became able to do everything alone, from examining the patient to assessment and planning, presenting at the conference, and writing in the chart, and I felt my growth and, though only a little, it also became my own confidence.

When I was doing clerkships in Japan, I judged that it was an infection just by looking at culture results. But as I was bombarded every day by the doctors with questions such as "Does the positive culture really mean infection?", "When and from where did that bacterium enter the body?", and "What are the appropriate type, dose and duration of antibiotics?", and looked things up and thought one by one, I was able to deeply learn the basics and the secret of infectious disease practice: appropriately interpreting and combining the patient's history, findings and test results, and deriving what is happening to the patient in front of me as a single story. I feel that this experience will be useful, not only as a single clerkship but as flesh and blood in my life as a doctor from now on.

Besides the infectious disease consult clerkship, I also had the chance to talk directly with world-famous infectious disease doctors, with the local hospital infection control staff (unlike in Japan, they were former nurses or graduates of schools of public health), and with a doctor who graduated from Nagoya University and is now a professor at Johns Hopkins University, as well as to attend lectures with local medical students. It was rare for them to speak to an exchange student on their own initiative, but when I went and spoke to them and asked questions, I was kindly welcomed and could hear all sorts of stories. While doing clerkships in an unfamiliar overseas hospital, I once again realized the importance of thinking for myself about what I want to do and taking action myself.

Although it was a short period of one month, I found gaps and on weekends traveled to nearby cities with my classmate 王, and relaxed in spare time with everything from sightseeing to watching sports and listening to music. Among them, my first musical in my life and watching sports such as the MLB and the NBA were tremendously powerful and a lot of fun. One Friday, my supervising doctor took me out for a drink at Happy Hour, and we had a lively time talking about his past research and his hometown. Going out to eat with a local medical student I met there and promising to meet again in Japan is also a good memory.

I would like to take this opportunity to thank everyone on the staff of the International Research Office, starting with Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川, who supported this very valuable experience, Dr. Itzel, who has taught medical English since I entered university, the doctors and staff of Johns Hopkins University who accepted me, 王, with whom I lived, and my parents. Thank you very much.
